question:
A 26-year-old pregnant woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 28 weeks of gestation, attends a routine prenatal
visit. She denies vaginal bleeding, cramping, fluid loss, or reduced fetal movement. Initial prenatal labs
showed an A-negative blood type, mild anemia, and positive IgG antibodies to Rhesus D, rubella, and
varicella, with negative syphilis, hepatitis B, and HIV screens. Her first pregnancy was complicated by
chronic placental abruption. Today, her vital signs are normal, and examination reveals a gravid
abdomen with a fundal height of 26 cm. Laboratory results show an anti-D antibody titer of 1:32.
Doppler velocimetry demonstrates peak blood flow velocity through the middle cerebral artery (MCA) at
two times the median, with normal flow in the umbilical arteries and ductus venosus. What is the most
appropriate next step in management? Answer Choices: (A) Serial MCA Doppler studies and
anticipated delivery at 37 weeks EGA (B) Amniocentesis for fetal lung maturity (C) Immediate cesarean
delivery (D) Percutaneous umbilical blood sampling (E) Expectant management with weekly non-stress
tests (F) Administration of anti-D immunoglobulin (G) Fetal steroids and delivery within 48 hours (H)
Serial umbilical artery Doppler studies (I) Intrauterine fetal blood transfusion (J) Fetal steroids and
delivery at 32 to 34 weeks EGA
 A. Intrauterine fetal blood transfusion
B. Percutaneous umbilical blood sampling
C. Fetal steroids and delivery at 32 to 34 weeks EGA
D. Amniocentesis for fetal lung maturity
E. Serial MCA Doppler studies and anticipated delivery at 37 weeks EGA
F. Administration of anti-D immunoglobulin
G. Expectant management with weekly non-stress tests
H. Immediate cesarean delivery
I. Serial umbilical artery Doppler studies
J. Fetal steroids and delivery within 48 hours
